title: How NRIs Can Lower the 30% TDS on Indian Rental Income and Claim Refunds
excerpt: Tenants must withhold 30% on rent paid to NRI landlords — but deductions, a lower-TDS certificate under Section 197, and a timely tax return can recover most of it.
body:
• Tenants must deduct 30% tax at source (31.2% with surcharge and cess) on rent paid to NRI landlords — regardless of the landlord's actual income — and deposit it with the government.
  • That headline rate usually overstates what you owe: a 30% standard deduction, municipal taxes, home-loan interest and other deductions bring the real liability well below the TDS cut.
  • NRIs can apply for a lower TDS certificate under Section 197 using Form 13, letting the tenant deduct at a reduced rate and freeing up cash flow through the year.
  • Any excess TDS can be claimed back by filing an Indian income tax return — but mismatches, late tenant deposits and non-filing are triggering notices and refund delays, according to recent reporting.

For many non-resident Indians, rent from a property back home is supposed to be steady, predictable income. In practice, the trouble starts the moment the tenant pays: by law, 30% is sliced off the top before the money ever reaches the landlord — and getting the excess back takes paperwork, patience, and a tax return filed in India.

Why so much is withheld upfront

When a tenant pays rent to an NRI landlord, tax must be deducted at source under Section 195 of the Income-tax Act at 30%, which rises to 31.2% once surcharge and the 4% health and education cess are added, according to a recent Economic Times report cited by Outlook Money. The cut applies no matter how much the landlord actually earns or what expenses they will later claim. The tenant is responsible for obtaining a Tax Deduction Account Number (TAN), filing Form 26Q quarterly, issuing Form 16A as proof of deduction, submitting Form 15CA before remitting rent, and obtaining Form 15CB from a chartered accountant if annual rent exceeds ₹5 lakh. The rent itself must land in the landlord's NRO account, unless it is paid from an NRE account by another NRI.

The mismatch between the withholding rate and the real liability is the heart of the problem. Rental income is taxed under "Income from House Property" at the same slab rates that apply to resident Indians — and the deductions available are generous.

What you can actually claim

The most valuable deduction is automatic: a 30% standard deduction on the Net Annual Value of the property under Section 24, available regardless of actual maintenance spending. On top of that, NRIs can deduct municipal taxes actually paid during the year, the full interest paid on a home loan for a let-out property, principal repayment of up to ₹1.5 lakh under Section 80C, and an additional ₹50,000 on the interest component under Section 80EE for qualifying loans. For NRIs in countries with a Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement with India — more than 90, including the US, UK, Canada and Australia — a foreign tax credit can be claimed abroad so the same income is not taxed twice. Filing an Indian return remains mandatory to use these benefits.

"If your actual tax liability is less than 31.2 percent, you can apply for a lower TDS certificate under Section 197 — it prevents funds from being blocked and lets you freely repatriate the money."

— Tax guidance for NRI landlords, via NBA Office

Two ways to get your money back

The first is proactive: apply for a lower TDS certificate under Section 197 by filing Form 13 with the assessing officer, submitting income estimates and supporting proof. Once granted, the certificate is shared with the tenant, who deducts at the approved lower rate for the rest of the year — improving monthly cash flow instead of locking money with the government.

The second is the refund route: file the income tax return (ITR-2 for NRIs with rental income) by the July 31 deadline, report the rental income accurately after deductions, and claim the excess TDS as a refund. Regularly checking Form 26AS ensures the TDS the tenant deposited actually shows up as your credit. Filing is required when total Indian income exceeds ₹2.5 lakh under the old regime or ₹3 lakh under the new regime.

Where it goes wrong

A September 2026 Outlook Money report found NRIs running into three recurring problems: TDS mismatches between what tenants deposited and what appears in Form 26AS, late deposits by tenants, and reconciliation issues that stall refunds. Tax notices are being triggered by non-filing, incorrect reporting of rental income, and NRO account violations. The fix is unglamorous but effective: a written lease that records NRI status, collecting and storing every Form 16A, verifying 26AS entries quarterly, and filing on time even when the numbers feel small. With the right paperwork, the 30% cut is a timing problem — not a tax bill.
